lines: Avery Brooks
+1 (555) 010-3319 | avery.brooks@example.com | example.com/in/abrooks
Date of birth: 9 Jan 1998 | Nationality: Brazilian
EDUCATION
Eastmoor University | B.S. in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Brightcart Retail | Data Analyst | Metro City, USA | Aug 2022 - Jun 2025
- Built the weekly retention dashboard for 2.4M customers that marketing used to retarget lapsed buyers, lifting 90-day repeat purchase from 22% to 27%.
- Cut the monthly revenue report from 3 days of spreadsheet work to 2 hours by moving it to scheduled SQL queries and a shared dashboard.
- Found customers with no orders by left-joining the orders table to the customers table and counting rows with a null customer name.

- Joining 40 source tables, deduplicating customer records across two loyalty systems and rebuilding the attribution logic in dbt-style SQL models, raised the share of orders tied to a campaign from 58% to 81%.
- Presented the quarterly customer review to the leadership team, and two of its three recommendations were funded in the next budget.
- Trained 20 merchandisers to answer their own questions with the self-serve dashboards, halving ad hoc data requests.
Pinecrest Insurance | Junior Analyst | Metro City, USA | Apr 2021 - Jul 2022
- Ran the checkout A/B test until significance by checking the p-value every day and stopping on the first day it fell below 0.05.
- Analyzed 18 months of call-center data; the findings moved two agents to the evening peak and cut average hold time from 9 to 5 minutes.
- Wrote the team's SQL style guide and review checklist, which cut query errors found in review by half.

- Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract while also maintaining the team calendar, answering ad hoc questions from sales, updating onboarding documents and covering the help desk on Fridays, which saved the fraud team 10 hours a month.
PROJECTS
City Bike-Share Demand Study | Independent Project | Python, SQL | Jan 2025 - Present
- Leveraged data-driven insights and advanced analytics to unlock actionable value for urban mobility stakeholders.
- Cut empty-station hours from 300 to 200 a week, a 50% reduction, in a replay of last summer's rebalancing.
- Raised forecast hit rate by 15% across 120 stations, from 60% to 75%, by adding weather and event features.
Food Pantry Visit Analysis | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Excel, SQL | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day, so the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut the Saturday line from 50 to 20 minutes.
- 9,000 handwritten visit logs were cleaned into a single table and repeat visitors were matched, so the pantry had its first count of unique households.
- Wrote a one-page guide the pantry coordinator used to update the visit table each month after the project ended.
SKILLS
Tools: SQL, Python, Excel
Methods: dashboards, forecasting, metric design, data-quality checks

items.says: Check that the profile link is live and leads to a complete, current profile.
items.because: It is the only supporting link provided.

items.says: Remove the date of birth and nationality for most U.S. applications unless requested.
items.because: They are generally unnecessary for assessing qualifications.

items.says: Separate the dashboard’s reach from its effect and avoid presenting the repeat-purchase increase as proven causal without evidence.
items.because: Other marketing changes could have affected the rate.

items.says: Specify your role in the migration if others built the scheduled queries or dashboard.
items.because: Ownership should be as clear as the result.

items.says: The stated left join and null customer-name check do not identify customers with no orders.
items.because: They can identify orders without a matching customer; the check should start with customers and look for a missing order ID.

items.says: Add the business use or scale of the customers-with-no-orders work, if there was one.
Shorten the list of implementation steps.
items.because: The result is a data-coverage measure, not necessarily a marketing result.

items.says: Clarify whether 58%–81% means improved matching of unattributed orders rather than improved campaign performance.
items.because: More orders tied to campaigns is not necessarily a marketing result.

items.says: Identify the recommendations’ subject or your analytical contribution.
items.because: Otherwise the bullet reads more like a presentation achievement than a data-analysis achievement.

items.says: Clarify the period and how the reduction in ad hoc requests was measured, if available.
items.because: That makes the impact easier to trust.

items.says: Daily p-value checks followed by stopping at the first result below 0.05 are not sound test practice.
items.because: That form of optional stopping can inflate false-positive risk.

items.says: Clarify whether the hold-time comparison covers comparable periods and whether other changes contributed.
items.because: The causal claim is stronger than the evidence shown.

items.says: Specify how the reduction in query errors found in review was measured.
items.because: “By half” is persuasive when the comparison is defined.

items.says: Remove or separate the unrelated duties and focus on the automation and time saved.
items.because: The long list hides the achievement and makes your contribution hard to scan.

items.says: Check that “Present” reflects ongoing work if the project is still in progress.
items.because: The project dates should be easy to reconcile with the reported results.

items.says: Replace the generic insights bullet with a concrete action or remove it.
items.because: It gives no method, deliverable, or result.

items.says: The reduction from 300 to 200 empty-station hours is 33%, not 50%.
items.because: The arithmetic needs correcting.

items.says: Make clear the reduction was in a replay or simulation, not observed in live operations.
items.because: Simulated and real-world impact are different.

items.says: The change from 60% to 75% is 15 percentage points, or a 25% relative increase, not an unqualified 15%.
items.because: Readers need to know what improved.

items.says: Define “hit rate” and explain how the forecast was evaluated.
items.because: Readers need to know whether the evaluation was credible.

items.says: Check that the wait times were measured comparably and that the shift move was the relevant intervention.
items.because: The result is strong if its basis is clear.

items.says: Change the passive construction to distinguish your contribution from the team’s.
items.because: Your ownership is unclear.

items.says: Explain how repeat visitors were matched if that method was meaningful to the work.
items.because: The scale is impressive, but your ownership is unclear.

items.says: Name a specific dashboard or modeling tool used instead of relying on broad terms such as “dashboards.”
items.because: Specific, defensible skills help a reviewer match you to a role.
